questions.question: Describe how astronomers discovered that the Milky Way is not the whole Universe, and explain what deep field images show about the number of galaxies.
questions.expected_answer: Astronomers had seen fuzzy spiral nebulae but did not know whether they were inside the Milky Way. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found individual stars of a known type (Cepheid variables) in the Andromeda Nebula and, from their brightness, showed it was far beyond the Milky Way, a separate galaxy (now about 2.5 million light years away). Deep field images, such as the Hubble Deep Field (1995, about 3 000 galaxies in a tiny apparently empty patch) and the James Webb deep field (2022), show galaxies in every direction; since such patches are typical, the observable Universe holds hundreds of billions (possibly up to about two trillion) galaxies.

questions.question: Name and describe the three main types of galaxies, giving an example of each where possible. Explain what the Local Group is.
questions.expected_answer: Spiral galaxies have a central bulge and a flat rotating disc with spiral arms rich in gas, dust and young blue stars, where new stars form; about two thirds have a central bar (e.g. the Milky Way, a barred spiral, and Andromeda). Elliptical galaxies are smooth, round or egg-shaped, with mostly old reddish stars and little gas, so few new stars form; they include the largest galaxies, giant ellipticals, often at the centres of clusters. Irregular galaxies have no regular shape, are usually small and gas-rich (e.g. the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds). The Local Group is the group of more than fifty galaxies, about ten million light years across, held together by gravity, to which the Milky Way belongs; its largest members are Andromeda, the Milky Way and the Triangulum Galaxy.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the expanding Universe and the observable Universe. State the age of the Universe and the size of the observable Universe, and explain why the observable Universe is wider than 2 × 13.8 billion light years.
questions.expected_answer: In 1929 Hubble found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they recede. Space itself is stretching, carrying galaxy groups apart (like raisins in rising bread: every raisin moves away from every other, with no centre). Tracing this back gives the Big Bang, the start of the expansion from a hot dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. The observable Universe is the region from which light has had time to reach us since then; the whole Universe may be larger. Because space has kept expanding while the light travelled, the objects whose light is now reaching us are now much further away, so the edge is about 46 billion light years away in every direction, a diameter of about 93 billion light years, not 27.6 billion.
